observation_summary: The compiler's string representation of record types (specifically in toAnnotationString) incorrectly truncates long type definitions with '...' or uses '?' for recursive types, leading to invalid externs and test failures.
reasoning_summary: The issue is a procedural logic error in how the compiler generates string representations for complex or recursive types. The code is attempting to summarize or truncate these types for display/annotation purposes, but the logic for this summarization is flawed, causing it to produce invalid output (e.g., '...' or '?') that breaks downstream compilation. This is a computational strategy error within the type-to-string conversion method, not a missing guard or a simple assignment error.
evidence_used: junit.framework.ComparisonFailure: expected:<{loop: [?], number: number, st...> but was:<{loop: [{...}], number: number, st...>
junit.framework.ComparisonFailure: expected:<...number, a4: number, [a5: number, a6: number]}> but was:<...number, a4: number, [...]}>
The code below the @typedef tries embedding the body of the @typedef and ends up truncating it if the length is too long with a '...'
evidence_gaps: The actual implementation of the toAnnotationString method is not provided in the snippets, only the test calls.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the truncation logic might involve a check for length, the core issue is the incorrect implementation of the string generation strategy itself, not just a missing or wrong guard.
This is a local procedural issue in how types are rendered to strings, not a missing design-level capability or class.
